title: Mnuchin's Plan to Gut Wall Street Safeguard Revealed!
text: Wall Street's big banks have a friend at the top. Dialing back the Volcker Rule, which limits banks' ability to make speculative bets, is a top priority for Steve Mnuchin, President Donald Trump's nominee for U.S. Treasury secretary, according to a document seen on Monday. In written answers to questions from members of the U.S. Senate Finance Committee, Mnuchin said he would use his role as head of the interagency Financial Stability Oversight Council to give the Volcker Rule a stricter definition of proprietary trading. What is "prop trading"? It is when a financial firm gambles its own money on privately held companies, hedge funds and similar vehicles. And the Volcker rule exists for a reason: it was designed to rein in exactly the kind of risk-taking that helped plunge banks into trouble during the financial crisis. Now listen to Mnuchin: "As Chair of FSOC I would plan to address the issue of the definition of the Volcker Rule to make sure that banks can provide the necessary liquidity for customer markets and address the issues in the Fed report," he wrote in the document, which also contained senators' questions and was verified by a Senate aide. At his confirmation hearing with the Senate Finance Committee last week, Mnuchin pointed to a recent Federal Reserve report that found the rule, part of the 2010 Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform law, was limiting market liquidity. The committee has not yet set a date to vote on sending the nomination to the full chamber for approval. His verdict? Regulators have applied proprietary trading bans to too many activities, he said. The Fed report found that ambiguity and gray areas in the rule were pushing dealers toward conservative strategies so they would not cross the line on the prohibitions. Too cautious for Wall Street!

title: North Korea Taunts Trump: Our Long-Range Missile Can Fly 'Anytime'!
text: It's a direct slap at the incoming president. Less than a week after Donald J. The next day Mr. Trump shot back on Twitter: "It won't happen!" Then came the defiant reply. On Sunday, an unidentified spokesman of the North Korean Foreign Ministry told the North's official Korean Central News Agency, "The ICBM will be launched anytime and anywhere determined by our supreme leadership." The spokesman's remarks, made public on the KCNA website Monday, were a response to comments last Thursday by Antony J. Blinken, the United States deputy secretary of state, that North Korea had made "a qualitative improvement" in its missile capabilities over the past year. Blinken also warned that Washington and its allies would keep up "comprehensive, sustained pressure and sanctions" against the North. And on NBC's "Meet the Press" on Sunday, Ashton B. Carter, the departing secretary of defense, issued a blunt warning: the United States would shoot down a North Korean missile "if it were coming towards our territory or the territory of our friends and allies." The chilling question remains unanswered: how close is North Korea to building a reliable ICBM?

title: Landslide! Macri Crushes Rivals as Fernandez Comeback Collapses
text: It was a rout. Candidates allied with Argentine President Mauricio Macri swept to victory in Sunday's mid-term election, tightening his grip on Congress and dealing a heavy blow to any comeback hopes of his predecessor Cristina Fernandez. Fernandez, a free-spending populist who nearly bankrupted the country during her 2007-2015 rule, limped home a distant second in her race for the Senate representing Buenos Aires, Argentina's most populous province. With 98 percent of ballots counted by the interior ministry, Macri's former education minister, Esteban Bullrich, had 41.34 percent against 37.27 percent for Fernandez in the province that is home to nearly 40 percent of Argentine voters. And it gets bigger. Macri's Cambiemos, or Let's Change, coalition captured all of the top five population centers: Buenos Aires City, and Buenos Aires, Cordoba, Santa Fe and Mendoza provinces. No single party had won all five in a mid-term vote since 1985! "Today the change elected in 2015 has been consolidated," Vice President Gabriela Michetti told voters. The results, largely in line with pre-vote opinion polls, stripped the opposition of the two-thirds majority it needs to block presidential vetoes, said Ignacio Labaqui, a local analyst with New York-based consultancy Medley Global Advisors. "This is a significant boost for the Macri administration, particularly because of the defeat of Cristina in Buenos Aires province," Labaqui said. Is Fernandez finished? Not quite: her second-place showing still hands her one of the province's three Senate seats under Argentina's list system. One third of the Senate and half of the house were up for election, and Macri's coalition will still lack a majority. The private sector has feared a political resurgence by Fernandez, who is adored by millions of low-income Argentines helped by generous social spending during her administrations.

text: Ai Wei-Wei tore into China's crackdown on lawyers and free speech on Wednesday, and he held out little hope that the coming Communist Party Congress would bring any new freedoms. The Chinese dissident artist spoke as he opened an exhibit in the Swiss city of Lausanne featuring some of his political works symbolizing repression. His charge was sweeping. "They are not accepting what we call common values such as democracy and freedom of speech and the freedom of religious practice and independence of the press or independence of a judicial system or people having the right to vote," Ai told a news conference. "China has been booming and become very powerful in the economic sense but at the same time it doesn't trust its own people," he said. "After 60 or 70 years in power, still its own people are not trusted to have a chance to vote." What about the five-yearly leadership reshuffle of the ruling Communist Party, set to begin on Oct. 18? Ai was scathing: "You have a party that functions more like a family. It doesn't matter how many meetings they have, it's always closed-door. So there's no trust remaining in society." On the same Wednesday, Human Rights Watch said China has launched tougher investigations into rights lawyers and law firms that take on politically sensitive issues. Ai, who lives in Berlin but returns to China regularly, voiced alarm about two friends, human rights lawyers ruthlessly thrown in jail for five and 10 years, respectively. Is he afraid? "So the danger is there but I have no fear for myself because I have been through everything and what I have done is not for myself. It's for my father's generation and my son's generation," the 60-year-old said.

title: Trump Hugs Harvey Victims in Make-or-Break Test of His Presidency!
text: Can Donald Trump play comforter-in-chief? The U.S. President took up the role of "comforter-in-chief" on a visit to storm-battered Houston, playing with children and serving food to evacuees from Hurricane Harvey, the first major natural disaster of his eight months in office. It was a closely watched test of his presidential mien. Earlier in the week he had been slammed for failing to show enough empathy to Texas residents during catastrophic flooding. This time Trump comforted victims and thanked volunteers and first responders. Trump, 71, was joined by his wife, Melania, as he handed out food and hugged, kissed and played with children at the "kid zone" in Houston's NRG Center, a vast 700,000-square-foot (65,000 square meter) facility that became the city's largest emergency shelter. It was a rare glimpse of Trump with everyday Americans away from his campaign-style rallies. The former real estate magnate looked relaxed as he posed for photographs with volunteers and chatted with evacuees alongside Texas Governor Greg Abbott. "It has been a wonderful thing," Trump said of meeting the children as he served food to evacuees amid shouts of "Thank you, sir." Trump, who declared Sunday a national day of prayer, also went to a church in nearby Pearland, where he and his wife helped load half a dozen cars with boxes of supplies for victims. His verdict on the volunteer work? "Good exercise." Trump also toured a neighborhood that had flooded but dried out, greeting residents and praising them for doing "a fantastic job holding it together." And the backdrop was devastating: a week of historic flooding that killed at least 40 people, displaced more than 1 million and dumped as much as 50 inches (127 cm) of rain!

title: Fired Up About Trump? Why Your Smartphone Won't Save Democracy
text: Whatever party you belong to, one thing is undeniable: Donald J. Trump's presidency has ignited political activism to a level of passion not seen since the civil rights movement. What is far less clear is what you can actually do about the Trump administration's changes. In an era that promises instant gratification, with cars, couriers and food summoned to your driveway at the tap of a smartphone app, you might think tech is a quick and easy route to becoming a political activist. Think again! Software and web tools can only take you so far. "Sitting behind your computer is not going to be as effective as showing up for people where they really need it," said Joshua Tauberer, the creator of GovTrack, a popular web tool for tracking legislation. "Government is people." At best, tech is a great resource for keeping on top of political activities. But sooner or later you will have to get outside or pick up the phone and engage with people, like fellow citizens and members of Congress. Does that mean tech is powerless? Not at all. Opponents of Mr. Trump's immigration ban used Twitter and Facebook to rally thousands of people for protests at the nation's airports last month. And protesters used social media platforms to help coordinate the Jan. 21 women's marches, which by one account were the largest day of demonstrations in American history. So what else can you do besides following news and events on Twitter and Facebook? Here is a guide to some of the most useful resources and tools I uncovered after interviewing activists. The first challenge to getting more politically active? Filtering out the flood of political news to figure out what you should care about.
